title: How to assign UPC codes for new marketplace listings
body_markdown:
Every new listing on Amazon, Walmart, or Google Shopping needs a valid UPC before it goes live — get the code wrong and your listing gets suppressed, flagged, or rejected outright. This guide walks through sourcing a legitimate UPC, assigning it correctly, and avoiding the mistakes that get sellers locked out of marketplaces in 2026.


**TL;DR**

- Buy UPCs only from GS1 US — third-party marketplaces sell recycled or fake codes that trigger listing suspensions.
- A standard UPC-A code is 12 digits; Amazon and Walmart both validate against the GS1 database before approving a new listing.
- Apply for a GTIN exemption if you make the product yourself — it skips the UPC requirement entirely for eligible categories.
- Assigning the same UPC to two different products is the #1 cause of catalog merge errors on Amazon in 2026.


## Why this matters

A UPC isn't paperwork — it's the identifier marketplaces use to match your product to their catalog, prevent duplicate listings, and route your item through their search index. Get it wrong and Amazon can suppress the listing, Walmart can reject the feed, or your item silently merges into someone else's product page.

Sellers running inventory across Amazon, eBay, Walmart, Shopify, and Etsy from one dashboard on [SellerChamp](https://sellerchamp.com/) run into UPC assignment constantly during bulk listing — one bad code in a CSV of 500 SKUs can stall an entire upload. Getting the assignment process right the first time saves the back-and-forth with marketplace support later.

## What you'll need

- A GS1 US company prefix (this is what makes your UPCs legitimate, not scraped or resold)
- A spreadsheet or bulk lister tool to track SKU-to-UPC pairs before upload
- Product dimensions and category info (some categories require GTIN exemption paperwork instead of a UPC)
- 15-30 minutes per new SKU batch, plus 24-48 hours if you're applying for a GTIN exemption
- Access to your marketplace seller account (Amazon Seller Central, Walmart Seller Center, etc.) to verify UPC acceptance before publishing

## The steps

### 1. Register for a GS1 US company prefix

This is the only source of legitimate UPCs — GS1 US is the sole official issuing body in North America. Buying UPCs from resale sites means you're licensing someone else's discontinued code, which is exactly what gets listings flagged for "UPC does not match brand" errors.

Registration runs through gs1us.org and typically takes a few business days to process. Your prefix determines how many unique product codes you can generate — a smaller prefix gives you fewer codes, so size the registration to your catalog, not just your current SKU count.

**Common mistake:** registering a prefix sized for 10 SKUs when you're planning to list 200 items across five marketplaces by year-end.

### 2. Generate UPC-A codes from your prefix

A UPC-A code is 12 digits: your company prefix, a product reference number, and a check digit calculated from the first 11. Most GS1 member portals generate the check digit automatically — don't hand-calculate it, a single wrong digit invalidates the whole code.

Assign codes sequentially and log them in a tracking sheet as you go. This prevents the single most common error sellers make: reusing a UPC on a second product because nobody remembered it was already assigned.

**Expected outcome:** every SKU in your catalog has one unique 12-digit UPC-A code, logged against the product name and internal SKU.

### 3. Match UPCs to SKUs before you touch the marketplace

Build your SKU-to-UPC map in a spreadsheet before uploading anything. Column one is your internal SKU, column two is the UPC, column three is the product title exactly as it'll appear on the listing.

This step catches duplicate or transposed codes while they're cheap to fix — a mismatch caught in a spreadsheet takes 30 seconds to correct; the same mismatch caught after an Amazon listing is live can take days of support tickets to resolve.

**Common mistake:** copy-pasting a UPC from an old, discontinued SKU into a new listing because the product looks similar.

### 4. Apply for a GTIN exemption if you manufacture the product

If you make the product yourself — no existing UPC anywhere in the supply chain — apply for a GTIN exemption instead of buying a code you don't need. Amazon's Brand Registry and GTIN Exemption tool both process this at the brand level, not per-SKU, so approval covers future listings under that brand.

The exemption typically clears in 24-48 hours once brand ownership is verified. Skipping this step and assigning a random UPC to a private-label product is a fast way to get a listing removed for "invalid GTIN."

**Expected outcome:** new listings publish without a UPC field error, tagged instead with your exemption approval.

### 5. Upload the listing with the UPC in the correct field

Each marketplace names the field differently — Amazon calls it "External Product ID," Walmart calls it "GTIN/UPC," Etsy doesn't require one at all for handmade goods. Map your spreadsheet's UPC column to the exact field name the marketplace's template expects.

Bulk upload tools that cross-list to Amazon, eBay, Walmart, and Shopify from one file cut this step from a per-marketplace chore to a single mapped upload — the field-matching logic runs once instead of four times.

**Common mistake:** pasting the UPC into a generic "Product ID" field that the marketplace doesn't actually validate, so the code never registers against the catalog.

### 6. Verify the code resolves before you go live

Scan or search the UPC against a barcode lookup database before publishing. If the code returns someone else's product, or returns nothing at all, stop and fix it — don't publish and hope the marketplace catches the error for you.

This 60-second check prevents the scenario where your new listing silently merges into an unrelated product's detail page because the UPC was already assigned to that item.

**Expected outcome:** the UPC resolves to your product name and brand, confirming it's clean before the listing goes public.

### 7. Monitor for catalog merge errors after launch

Check your new listings 24-48 hours after publishing. Amazon in particular will merge listings that share a UPC, even accidentally, and the merge doesn't always throw an obvious error — sometimes it just shows up as your title and images disappearing from a product page you didn't create.

Catching a merge in the first two days means a quick support ticket. Catching it three weeks later means untangling sales history, reviews, and Buy Box eligibility that got mixed with someone else's listing.

## Troubleshooting

**"UPC does not match brand" rejection on Amazon.** The code you're using is registered to a different brand in GS1's database, often because it was resold or reused from a discontinued product. Generate a new code from your own prefix and resubmit.

**Listing merges into an unrelated product page.** Two SKUs share the same UPC. Pull both listings, generate a fresh unique code for the newer one, and file a catalog correction request with the marketplace before republishing.

**GTIN exemption request denied.** Amazon usually denies exemptions when brand ownership isn't verified or the category requires a UPC regardless of manufacturing status (some restricted categories don't allow exemptions at all). Check the category's specific GTIN policy before reapplying.

**Walmart feed rejects the entire batch over one bad UPC.** Walmart's bulk feed validation fails the whole file on a single malformed code in many templates. Isolate the bad row, fix the check digit, and resubmit the corrected file rather than the whole batch again.

**Barcode won't scan at fulfillment centers.** This usually means the UPC-A was printed at the wrong size or resolution, not that the code itself is wrong. Reprint at 100% scale per GS1's barcode quality guidelines before sending inventory to FBA.

**Duplicate UPC across two of your own SKUs.** This happens most often when a spreadsheet gets copy-pasted mid-catalog-build. Reassign one SKU a fresh code from your prefix and update every marketplace listing using the old, conflicting code.

## Tools and resources

- GS1 US member portal — for prefix registration and UPC-A generation
- A barcode lookup tool — to verify a code resolves correctly before publishing
- Amazon's GTIN Exemption tool inside Seller Central — for brand-level exemption requests
- A SKU-to-UPC tracking spreadsheet — the single source of truth before any bulk upload
- [SellerChamp](https://sellerchamp.com/) — for mapping UPC fields once and cross-listing to Amazon, eBay, Walmart, and Shopify without repeating the field-matching work per marketplace

## What to do next

Once your UPC assignment process is clean, the next failure point is usually inventory sync — a listing with a correct UPC still oversells if stock counts aren't updating across marketplaces in real time. Fix the UPC layer first; it's the foundation everything else in your catalog sits on for 2026 and beyond.

## FAQ


**Do I need a UPC for every marketplace listing in 2026?**

Amazon and Walmart require a UPC or GTIN exemption for most new listings in 2026, while Etsy and eBay allow listings without one in many categories. Check each marketplace's specific catalog policy before publishing, since requirements vary by product type.

**Can I buy UPC codes from a reseller instead of GS1?**

Buying from a reseller instead of GS1 US is the most common cause of "UPC does not match brand" rejections. Resold codes are often recycled from discontinued products still registered to another brand.

**What's the difference between a UPC and a GTIN?**

A UPC-A is a 12-digit code and one specific type of GTIN (Global Trade Item Number), which is the umbrella term marketplaces use across 12-, 13-, and 14-digit formats. Amazon's listing fields typically ask for GTIN and accept UPC as one valid format.

**How long does a GS1 US prefix registration take?**

GS1 US prefix registration typically processes within a few business days in 2026. Generating individual UPCs from an approved prefix is instant once the registration clears.

**Why did my Amazon listing merge with someone else's product?**

Listings merge when two products share the same UPC in Amazon's catalog, even if the duplication was accidental. Generate a new unique code and file a catalog correction request to separate the listings.

**Is a GTIN exemption better than buying a UPC?**

A GTIN exemption is the right move only if you manufacture the product yourself with no existing UPC anywhere in its supply chain. If the product already has a manufacturer UPC, using that code is required, not an exemption.

**Can one UPC cover multiple product variations, like different colors?**

No, each variation, including color and size, needs its own unique UPC in most marketplace catalogs. Assigning one UPC across multiple variations is a common cause of listing errors on Amazon and Walmart.

**What happens if I skip UPC assignment entirely?**

Skipping UPC assignment on a marketplace that requires one blocks the listing from publishing at all, or gets it suppressed shortly after going live. Categories without a UPC requirement still benefit from one for cross-marketplace catalog matching.


## One last thing

The single biggest UPC mistake sellers make isn't a bad code — it's tracking UPCs per marketplace instead of per SKU. One product, one UPC, used identically on Amazon, Walmart, and everywhere else keeps the catalog matching clean; a different code per platform for the same physical product is what causes inventory sync tools to double-count stock in 2026.
